You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
We once spent six weeks building a feature customers had asked for.

The request appeared in interviews, support tickets, and sales calls. It seemed obvious: people wanted more control, so we built a flexible set of options, added permissions, polished the interface, and announced the release.

Almost nobody used it.

At first, we blamed discoverability. We added tooltips, emails, and in-app prompts. Usage barely moved.

The real problem was simpler. We had listened to what customers said they wanted, but we had not understood the job they were trying to do. They did not actually want more control. They wanted to feel confident that the default behavior would work without creating problems.

We had built a better steering wheel for people who wanted a reliable train.

That experience changed how I think about customer requests. A request is evidence, not a specification. It points to friction, but it does not always identify the right solution.

Now, before committing to a feature, I try to ask a few more questions. What happened right before someone asked for this? What are they doing today instead? How often does the problem occur? What would improve if we solved it? Can we test the behavior with a manual process or a rough prototype first?

Shipping something nobody uses is painful, but it can be valuable if it improves the way you build.

The lesson was not to ignore customers. It was to listen more carefully, test assumptions earlier, and measure success by changed behavior rather than shipped code.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Last quarter I shipped a feature I was genuinely proud of. People kept saying our reporting felt limited, so I built a flexible query builder that let them mix metrics, add custom filters, and save their own views. I spent nights on the UI and made sure the queries actually ran fast. We launched it with a short note in the product and a line in the changelog.

Two weeks later I looked at the numbers. Almost nobody had opened it. A few clicks on day one, then nothing. I sat there feeling stupid. All that work and it might as well have been invisible.

I messaged a few customers I thought would love it. Their answers were consistent and a little embarrassing. They did not want more flexibility. They wanted the three reports they already used to load faster and to export them without extra steps. The fancy builder solved a problem they did not have.

What stuck with me is this. I had been talking to the product more than I had been talking to people. I assumed a request for better reporting meant they wanted power. It meant they wanted less friction on the work they already did every week. Shipping something is easy to celebrate. Watching it sit unused is the part that actually teaches you.

Next time I will talk to five users before I write a single ticket. I will ask what they did last Tuesday instead of what they wish they could do someday. And I will treat usage, not launch day, as the real finish line.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Generic anecdote with no specific product, feature name, or concrete context
tells_B: Signposting ('What stuck with me is this')
